SK4021 The private method does not use instance state

A private instance method whose body never touches this can be static, which drops the hidden argument and the null check.

CategoryPerformance
Default severityhint
ScopeSemantic
Needs a compilationyes
Runs under --load=looseno
Cached per fileyes
Fixyes, safe
Language version floor—
Since1.3
ReSharperMemberCanBeMadeStatic.Local (resharper_member_can_be_made_static_local_highlighting)

Why

An instance call passes a this argument the method does not read and, through a reference, carries a null check the callee cannot avoid. Making the method static removes both, and the declaration then states the fact the body already established: this code depends on its arguments and on nothing else. That is the larger half of the value — a reader no longer has to read the body to learn whether the method participates in the object's state, and a later edit that starts using a field is rejected at the point it is written. The rule is deliberately restricted to private methods, where the change is invisible outside the type; static on a visible member is an API change and a different decision.

Example

Instead of:

sealed class Report {
    readonly string title;

    string Format(int count) => count + " rows";
}

Write:

sealed class Report {
    readonly string title;

    static string Format(int count) => count + " rows";
}

When it does not fire

Only an ordinary private method with a body, in a non-partial class, struct or record declared once in one file, is considered. static, abstract, virtual, override, partial, extern and new declarations are excluded, as is anything carrying an attribute — a serialization callback, a marked event handler and a framework-invoked method are all shapes where the signature is a contract rather than a choice. The body is walked with the same proof SK4020 uses, so any this, base, instance member or unresolved name withholds the finding; a recursive call to the method itself is admitted, because the fix makes that call static too. ⚠ Every call site in the file is then checked, and a single this.Method() or instance.Method() withholds the finding, because that spelling does not compile against a static method. ⚠ What the rule cannot see is reflection: a private method found by name through MethodInfo and invoked with an instance target breaks when it becomes static, and no analyzer can prove the absence of that. It also cannot see another file, which is why a partial containing type is excluded rather than analysed.
